title: 7 Habits of Highly Effective Generative AI Evaluations - Justin Muller

primary.label: Evaluation, Testing & Benchmarking

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The entire talk is about designing evaluation frameworks, using LLM judges, building gold standard test sets, and measurement methodology for GenAI systems. The speaker draws from over 100 evaluation frameworks across all industries at AWS, making this cross-domain methodology rather than a single vertical application. Evaluations are framed as a pre-deployment gate and ongoing development practice, with the case study progressing from 22% accuracy through iterative fixes to production launch. The talk assumes familiarity with ML metrics, prompt chaining, and RAG architectures but explains concepts accessibly with analogies like professor grading essays. This is a conference presentation delivered at the AI Engineer channel with slides, case studies, and a visual pipeline walkthrough. All ten evidence anchors are direct transcript excerpts with specific character ranges and grade 'said_in_transcript'.

summary: Justin Mohler, a Principal Applied AI Architect at AWS with 15 years of NLP experience, identifies evaluations as the number one gap preventing generative AI projects from scaling. He opens with a customer case: a document-processing workload with six to eight engineers stuck at 22% accuracy and facing cancellation. The root cause was zero evaluations—only a single end-to-end accuracy number. After designing an evaluation framework, the team reached 92% accuracy by January and launched as the largest document processing workload on AWS in North America at the time. Mohler argues evaluations serve three purposes—discovering problems (primary), suggesting solutions via GenAI reasoning (second), and measuring quality (distant third). He uses willingness to invest in gold-standard eval sets as his team's primary filter for project selection; teams unwilling to invest are running 'science projects.' He addresses traditional ML practitioners' anxiety about free-text outputs by drawing an analogy to professors grading essays: good professors explain what went wrong, not just assign a number. Two vivid examples reinforce that reasoning matters as much as output: a 2x4 with a correctly drilled hole may have been produced dangerously, and a meteorology company's summarizer output 'sunny and bright' despite rainy sensor data, with flawed reasoning about mental health. Prompt decomposition is a prerequisite because evaluations can only attach to a whole prompt. A weather company example shows decomposition in action: Claude couldn't reliably compare wind speeds (saying 7 < 5), so the team replaced that step with a Python mathematical comparison, achieving 100% accuracy. Semantic routing—directing easy tasks to small models and hard tasks to large models—benefits from per-step evaluation and removes 'dead space' tokens that confuse models and increase cost. Mohler then presents the seven habits common to successfully scaled GenAI evaluations: fast (30-second target via parallel generation, judging, and summarizing), quantifiable (produce numbers, average across numerous test cases to smooth jitter), explainable (evaluate reasoning of both generation and judge using rubrics), segmented (evaluate each step individually, choose the smallest appropriate model per step), diverse (cover all use cases with ~100 test cases), and traditional (use numeric evaluation for numeric outputs, RAG retrieval metrics, cost and latency measurements—don't force GenAI where traditional techniques suffice). He concludes with a visual walkthrough of the evaluation pipeline: start with a gold standard set (the most important investment), feed inputs through a prompt template into an LLM to generate output with reasoning, compare against the gold standard answer using a judge prompt that produces a number and reasoning, then break results down by category for right and wrong answers. He strongly warns against using GenAI to create gold standard sets—it propagates the same errors into the system—but allows a 'silver standard' set (GenAI-generated, human-reviewed) as a partial aid.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

takeaways: Evaluations are the number one missing piece preventing GenAI projects from scaling; cost, hallucinations, and capacity are secondary concerns.
The primary goal of an evaluation framework is to discover problems and suggest fixes—not merely to produce a quality score.

Gold standard evaluation sets are the single most important investment; using GenAI to create them propagates its errors throughout the system. A human-reviewed 'silver standard' set is a partial alternative.
Prompt decomposition enables per-step evaluation and allows replacing GenAI with traditional code (e.g., Python for math comparisons), as demonstrated by a weather company achieving 100% accuracy.

Evaluations must be fast (30-second target), quantifiable (averaged across diverse test cases), explainable (rubric-based reasoning from generation and judge), and segmented (per-step model selection).
Traditional evaluation techniques (numeric comparison, RAG retrieval/precision/F1, cost, latency) should not be abandoned in favor of GenAI-only approaches.
Evaluating only output is dangerous—reasoning must also be evaluated, as correct output from flawed reasoning hides systemic defects.
Evaluations are the best filter for separating science projects from projects that will scale; teams unwilling to invest in evals rarely succeed.
Understand why evaluations are the critical bottleneck for scaling GenAI workloads
Distinguish evaluation frameworks designed for problem discovery from those designed for quality measurement

sections.title: Speaker Introduction and Background
sections.summary: Justin Mohler introduces himself as a Principal Applied AI Architect at AWS with degrees in physics, math, law, and business. His small specialist team helps customers scale GenAI workloads across all industries and sizes, giving him visibility into both successful and failed projects and the best practices that distinguish them.

sections.title: Evaluations as the Biggest Challenge in Scaling GenAI
sections.summary: Mohler identifies evaluations as the number one challenge in scaling GenAI, ranking above cost, hallucinations, accuracy, and capacity. He calls evaluations the 'missing piece' that, when added, unlocks the ability to scale workloads that otherwise stall.

sections.title: Customer Case Study: Document Processing Workload
sections.summary: A July 2024 escalation involved a document-processing workload with six to eight engineers stuck at 22% accuracy and facing cancellation. The team had zero evaluations—only a single end-to-end accuracy number. After designing an evaluation framework, problems became visible and trivial to fix, reaching 92% accuracy by January and launching as the largest document processing workload on AWS in North America.

sections.title: Three Purposes of Evaluation Frameworks
sections.summary: Mohler reframes evaluation goals: discovering problems is primary, suggesting solutions via GenAI reasoning is second, and measuring quality is a distant third. The design mindset—finding errors versus scoring quality—fundamentally changes the framework produced.

sections.title: Evaluations as the Project Success Filter
sections.summary: Mohler uses evaluations as his team's strict filter for project selection. Teams unwilling to spend two hours building gold-standard eval sets are running 'science projects'; teams that volunteer four hours are the ones achieving 100x ROI or dramatic cost reductions.

sections.title: Free Text Evaluation Analogy: Professor Grading Essays
sections.summary: Traditional ML practitioners' anxiety about free-text evaluation is misplaced. Humanity has graded free text for centuries. Bad professors give only scores; good professors explain what went wrong and how to improve—GenAI evaluations should do the same.

sections.title: Why Reasoning Matters: 2x4 and Meteorology Examples
sections.summary: A 2x4 with a correctly drilled hole may have been produced by a dangerous methodology. Similarly, a meteorology company's summarizer output 'sunny and bright' despite rainy sensor data, with reasoning that 'it's important to mental health to be happy.' Evaluating only output misses such defects; correct output from flawed reasoning is equally dangerous.

sections.title: Prompt Decomposition as Prerequisite for Evaluation
sections.summary: Since evaluations can only attach to a whole prompt, large complex prompts make it difficult to isolate errors. Prompt decomposition breaks prompts into evaluable components, likened to using a multimeter to sense across a circuit rather than at a single point.

sections.title: Weather Company Prompt Decomposition Example
sections.summary: The same weather company had a wind-speed comparison step in their prompt (less than 5 = not windy, more than 5 = windy). When scaling, Claude occasionally failed the math—saying 7 is less than 5—about 2-3% of the time. By decomposing the prompt into a chaining series and replacing the mathematical comparison with Python, that step's accuracy went to 100%. Decomposition also lets teams decide whether GenAI is even the right tool for each step.

sections.title: Semantic Routing and Per-Step Evaluation
sections.summary: Semantic routing—directing easy tasks to small models and hard tasks to large models based on input complexity—is a very common pattern. Attaching evals to each step (the router output is just a number like 1 or 2) significantly increases accuracy by removing 'dead space'—unnecessary instructions for tasks that don't need them, which add cost and confusion opportunities.

sections.title: Seven Habits Introduction and Habit 1: Fast
sections.summary: Mohler introduces the seven most common trends across successfully scaled GenAI workloads. Habit one is fast: evaluation frameworks should operate in seconds, not weeks. A team getting weekly results makes few iterations; a team with a 30-second framework makes hundreds of changes daily. The 30-second target breaks into 10 seconds parallel generation across 100 test cases, 10 seconds parallel judging against gold standard, and 10 seconds summarizing results by category.

sections.title: Habit 2: Quantifiable
sections.summary: Effective frameworks produce numbers. GenAI scores have jitter (like a professor grading differently after wine), but averaging across numerous diverse test cases smooths it out. Building 100 test cases also surfaces product design debates—e.g., whether to answer tax questions or redirect them—clarifying project scope and ensuring out-of-scope questions are tested.

sections.title: Habit 3: Explainable
sections.summary: Evaluations must examine how the model reasons, not just outputs. The judge's reasoning also needs attention—engineers must prompt-engineer the judge just as they do the generation prompt. Using rubrics (like a professor's grading criteria: length, sources, tone) gives the judge clear instructions and asking it to explain its reasoning is good prompt engineering for the judge.

sections.title: Habit 4: Segmented
sections.summary: Almost all scaled workloads are multi-step, so each step must be evaluated individually. This lets teams prove the smallest appropriate model for each step—for example, using Nova Micro for a simple semantic router that outputs 1, 2, 3.

sections.title: Habit 5: Diverse and Habit 6: Traditional
sections.summary: Diverse means covering all use cases with ~100 test cases (fewer for edge cases). Traditional means not throwing out proven techniques: use numeric evaluation for numeric outputs, RAG retrieval/precision/F1 metrics for database accuracy, and traditional cost and latency measurements. Don't force GenAI where it isn't needed.

sections.title: Visual Walkthrough of the Evaluation Pipeline and Conclusion
sections.summary: Mohler walks through the evaluation pipeline visually. Start with a gold standard set—the most important time investment since the entire system is designed around it. He strongly warns against using GenAI to create gold standard sets, because if GenAI introduces errors, the system optimizes toward those same errors. A 'silver standard' set (GenAI-generated guesses, human-reviewed) can help but cannot replace human-verified gold standards. The pipeline proceeds: take an input from the gold standard set, feed it through a prompt template into an LLM to generate an output with answer and reasoning, compare the generated output against the matching gold standard answer using a judge prompt (which produces a number and its reasoning), pull the category from the gold standard set, and generate a summary of right and wrong answers broken down by category. He concludes the talk and invites questions.
